title: Embodied VLAs: RT-2, OpenVLA, π0, GR00T

questions.question: What makes a vision-language-action model different from a VLM that only answers questions?
options: It uses a language model only to summarize the robot's trajectory.
It converts the robot camera into a text-only classification label.
It takes action logs and outputs only image captions.
It takes images and instructions, then outputs robot actions such as joint targets.
questions.explanation: A VLA conditions on both what the robot sees and the language instruction, then emits a control action such as joint targets or an end-effector pose. The image-classification option stops at a label, so it does not provide the action output that distinguishes a VLA.

questions.question: RT-2 quantizes each normalized action dimension into 256 bins. For a 10-DOF action at one control step, how many action tokens are emitted?
options: 1 token, because all dimensions share one bin.
256 tokens, one for every possible bin.
30 tokens, one for each control frequency unit.
10 tokens, one per action dimension.
questions.explanation: Each action dimension is independently mapped to one quantized vocabulary ID at a control step. For a 10-dimensional action, that is 10 emitted tokens; the 256 bins are the available values per dimension, not 256 outputs.

questions.question: What does FAST do to compress a sequence of continuous robot actions?
options: Encode each joint value as one of 256 uniform bins at every step.
Predict a 50-step action sequence with a diffusion loss.
Apply a DCT, keep selected frequency coefficients, then quantize them.
Run a VQ image tokenizer over the robot camera frames.
questions.explanation: FAST applies a discrete cosine transform to each action trajectory, retains selected frequency coefficients, and quantizes them, reducing the autoregressive sequence. Uniform per-step bins in the first option describe the RT-2/OpenVLA representation rather than FAST.

questions.question: How does pi0 produce smooth continuous actions according to the lesson?
options: A text decoder predicts captions that a separate controller converts to torque.
A language model generates one discrete joint token at a time for all 50 steps.
A VQ codebook selects a single image patch for each robot joint.
A small action expert uses flow matching to emit a 50-step sequence in a few denoising steps.
questions.explanation: The π0 action expert reads the VLM's hidden states and uses rectified flow to emit a continuous 50-step action sequence in a few denoising steps. Per-joint discrete tokens are the RT-2-style alternative and retain quantization rather than this continuous action formulation.

questions.question: A humanoid needs slow scene-level planning and fast full-body control. Which GR00T N1 component split fits?
options: System 1 plans at 1 Hz; System 2 emits 100 Hz joint commands.
A frozen VLM directly controls every joint without an action head.
System 2 plans subgoals; System 1 controls joints quickly.
Both systems generate the same action tokens at the same frequency.
questions.explanation: GR00T assigns slow scene-level subgoal planning to the large System 2 VLM at about 1 Hz and fast joint control to the smaller System 1 action transformer at 50–100 Hz. The reversed-frequency option would put slow planning in the time-sensitive control path.

questions.question: A robot must follow a novel phrasing such as 'pick the third largest object from the left.' Why mix web VQA with robot demonstrations during training?
options: Web VQA replaces the need for robot action trajectories.
Co-fine-tuning preserves general language knowledge while grounding it in robot actions.
Robot-only data guarantees broad language understanding from action tokens alone.
The mixture lets the robot ignore image observations during control.
questions.explanation: Web VQA examples retain broad language and visual knowledge, while robot demonstrations teach how instructions map to actions; mixing them helps transfer to novel phrasing. The robot-only guarantee option contradicts the lesson's warning that robot-only models can fail on out-of-distribution instructions.
